paper.citation: Bishop C, Clarke R, Freitas TT, Arruda AFS, Guerriero A, Ramos MS, Pereira LA, Loturco I. Change-of-Direction Deficit vs. Deceleration Deficit: A Comparison of Limb Dominance and Inter-limb Asymmetry between Forwards and Backs in Elite Male Rugby Union Players. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2020 (published online 29 Dec 2020).
paper.abstract: A cross-sectional correlational study of 25 elite male rugby union players (13 forwards, 12 backs) from one professional team, tested at the end of pre-season. It compared limb dominance and inter-limb asymmetry for the change-of-direction (COD) deficit and deceleration (DEC) deficit, and their associations with jump, linear sprint and power tests.
paper.tldr: In elite rugby union players, the faster limb often differed between the COD-deficit and DEC-deficit, and neither deficit measure correlated with jump performance, so each may need its own profiling.
paper.methods: Players completed squat, countermovement and drop jumps, a 15-m sprint, the 505 COD test, and half squat and jump squat mean propulsive power in one session. COD-deficit and DEC-deficit were calculated for each limb; kappa coefficients compared limb dominance and asymmetry direction, Pearson and Spearman correlations were run, and independent t-tests with Hedges g compared forwards and backs.
paper.findings: Limb dominance agreement between the COD-deficit and DEC-deficit was moderate (kappa 0.41 left, 0.48 right). Backs were faster over 15 m (effect size -0.86) and had higher countermovement jump, reactive strength index, half squat and jump squat power than forwards (effect sizes 0.86 to 0.94), but COD and DEC deficits did not differ by position. Significant jump correlations with linear and 505 times were moderate to large (r about -0.41 to -0.68), while no jump test correlated significantly with the COD-deficit, DEC-deficit or their asymmetries.
paper.limitations: The study was under-powered, with 12 to 13 players per position against an a priori requirement of 21 per group. It was cross-sectional, tested at a single pre-season time point, and drawn from one team, so associations apply only to this population. Ground contact time and DEC-deficit reliability CVs exceeded 10%, and small absolute deficit values inflate asymmetry percentages.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can profile change of direction using both the COD-deficit and DEC-deficit, since the faster limb can differ between them and neither tracks jump scores. Deficit-based asymmetry percentages are inflated by small absolute values, so chasing perfect symmetry on them is not advised. Backs and forwards differ in linear speed and jump power but not in these deficit measures.
paper.athleteDev: The paper supports profiling change of direction with both the COD-deficit and DEC-deficit because they can identify different limb dominance and are not explained by jump tests. Backs were faster over 15 m and more powerful in jumps than forwards, which can inform positional profiles, but the deficit measures did not differ by position.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy players with no injuries in the prior six weeks and did not examine injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or to interpret limb asymmetry after injury.
